sourceBindings.text: Enlarged teaching models: cereal fibrous roots, possible legume nodules, carrot storage taproot and a strawberry plant. No scale, measured depth, fixed soil texture, species identification or nitrogen amount is represented. All information is also written below.
Cereal: many branching fibrous roots; residue effects depend on management.
Legume: enlarged example nodules on lateral roots; their presence alone does not measure fixation.
Carrot: enlarged edible taproot with a sufficiently loose rooting space; no mandatory texture.
Strawberry: low herbaceous fruit crop, not a tree; site and drainage still need evidence.
Explain what the model shows and what it cannot prove
Describe cereal roots, a possible legume nodule and the carrot taproot.
Give one site-suitability or measured-depth claim this model cannot prove.
Recognize the three structures but do not infer grains must grow in sand or fruit in clay.

sourceBindings.text: Legumes are valued as protein-rich food crops; the crop’s use still distinguishes dry pulses, oilseed and forage legumes.
Vegetables contribute vitamins, minerals and fibre; crop cycles and nutrient needs vary widely.
Many fruit crops are valued for sweetness, vitamins and antioxidants. Nutritional and management characteristics vary by crop.

Another classification can group carrots, potatoes and beets as root and tuber vegetables. That is a grouping by harvested parts and use, not a claim that all three are botanical roots. It illustrates a different classification lens; it is not an Egyptian regulatory list.
